metadata.description: 29 UK & Ireland wildlife species curated for maximum ecological web connectivity
sources: Mammal Society Red List for Britain (2020)

conservationStatus.trendDetail: Threatened by Acute Oak Decline (AOD) and grey squirrel bark stripping

species.tagline: Supports 2,300+ species — the backbone of British woodland
species.description: A single mature oak supports more life than any other native tree: over 2,300 species including 38 birds, 1,178 invertebrates, and 326 species found on no other tree. Oaks are the structural foundation of lowland British woodland, providing food (acorns), nesting cavities, and the canopy architecture that shapes entire forest ecosystems.
species.keyFact: 326 species in the UK are found only on oak trees
species.keySource: Mitchell et al. (2019) Biological Conservation — PuRpOsE project

conservationStatus.trendDetail: −92% since grey squirrel introduction; ~287,000 remain vs 2.7M greys

species.tagline: Outnumbered 10:1 by an invasive rival carrying a lethal virus
species.description: Once ubiquitous across Britain, red squirrels have been pushed to Scotland, parts of northern England, and isolated island populations by competition with grey squirrels and the lethal squirrelpox virus. They play a vital role in woodland regeneration through acorn and seed caching — forgotten caches germinate into new trees.
species.keyFact: Squirrelpox virus accelerates grey squirrel replacement 20× faster than competition alone
species.keySource: Gurnell et al. (2004) Journal of Animal Ecology 73:26–35

conservationStatus.trendDetail: ~2.7 million in UK; introduced 1876–1929 from North America

species.tagline: An invasive species unravelling British woodland from within
species.description: Introduced from North America in the Victorian era, grey squirrels now outnumber native reds 10:1. They carry squirrelpox virus (harmless to greys, ~100% fatal to reds), strip bark from young trees causing £37M annual damage, and outcompete reds for acorns by digesting tannins more efficiently. Their impact cascades through the entire woodland ecosystem.
species.keyFact: Bark stripping causes £37 million annual damage to British woodlands
species.keySource: Tompkins et al. (2002) Proceedings of the Royal Society B 269:529–533

conservationStatus.trendDetail: Population stable; critical role in oak regeneration

species.tagline: The bird that planted Britain's oak forests after the Ice Age
species.description: Jays are the primary long-distance dispersal agent for oak acorns. A single jay can cache up to 5,000 acorns per autumn, burying them up to several kilometres from the parent tree. Forgotten caches germinate — this mechanism drove the northward expansion of oak forests after the last Ice Age. Without jays, oak regeneration would be dramatically slower.
species.keyFact: A single jay caches up to 5,000 acorns per autumn
species.keySource: Bossema (1979) Behaviour 70:1–116

conservationStatus.trendDetail: −51% since 1970; linked to prey and habitat loss

species.tagline: Britain's most familiar owl is quietly disappearing
species.description: The tawny owl is Britain's most common owl, yet its population has halved since 1970. It depends on mature trees with natural cavities for nesting — predominantly old oaks — and feeds on a wide variety of prey including voles, frogs, earthworms, and occasionally squirrels and jays. Its decline reflects broader changes in woodland health and prey availability.
species.keyFact: Population has halved (−51%) since 1970
species.keySource: Southern (1954) Ibis 99:384–410

conservationStatus.trendDetail: Population approximately doubled to ~562,000

species.tagline: A protected predator whose success creates pressure on hedgehogs
species.description: Badgers are Britain's largest land predator and one of its most iconic mammals. Highly social, they live in extended family groups in underground sett systems. Their diet is dominated by earthworms (~80%) supplemented by beetles, fruits, and small mammals. Their population growth, combined with habitat fragmentation, has intensified competition with hedgehogs — a classic intraguild predation relationship.
species.keyFact: A single badger can eat several hundred earthworms in one night
species.keySource: Neal & Cheeseman (1996) Badgers, Poyser

conservationStatus.trendDetail: Threatened by hybridisation with Spanish bluebell

species.tagline: Half the world's bluebells grow in Britain — an ancient woodland indicator
species.description: The UK holds approximately half the global population of native bluebells. They are an indicator of ancient woodland, taking advantage of the brief spring window when deciduous oak canopy allows sunlight to reach the forest floor. They provide critical early-season nectar for bumblebees emerging from hibernation and depend on earthworm-enriched soils for growth.
species.keyFact: The UK holds roughly half the world's population of native bluebells
species.keySource: Natural England ancient woodland indicators

species.tagline: From 30 million to less than a million in a human lifetime
species.description: Britain's most beloved mammal has undergone a catastrophic decline. Hedgehogs consume vast quantities of slugs, snails, beetles, and earthworms — earning the title 'the gardener's friend.' Their decline is driven by a perfect storm: agricultural intensification removing hedgerow habitat, road mortality, garden fencing blocking movement corridors, and increased competition/predation from rising badger populations.
species.keyFact: Population has fallen from ~30 million in the 1950s to fewer than 900,000
species.keySource: PTES State of Britain's Hedgehogs (2022)

conservationStatus.trendDetail: Recovered from historic lows thanks to nest box schemes; still weather-vulnerable

species.tagline: A conservation success story — recovered through community nest box schemes
species.description: The barn owl is one of Britain's most recognisable birds, hunting silently over farmland at dusk. After severe declines in the 20th century due to pesticide use and loss of old farm buildings, dedicated nest box programmes have supported recovery. They depend on rough grassland margins with high vole populations, and are vulnerable to harsh winters and loss of foraging habitat.
species.keyFact: A breeding pair and their young can consume ~4,000 prey items per year
species.keySource: BTO Breeding Bird Survey

conservationStatus.trendDetail: −60% since mid-1980s; iconic farmland bird decline

species.tagline: The soundtrack of the British countryside is falling silent
species.description: The skylark's ascending song flight was once the definitive sound of British farmland. Their 60% decline epitomises the broader collapse of farmland biodiversity driven by intensified agriculture — autumn sowing eliminates winter stubble foraging, tighter crop spacing prevents nesting, and pesticides reduce invertebrate food. They are a sentinel species: when skylarks decline, the farmland ecosystem is in trouble.
species.keyFact: Skylark populations have fallen 60% since the mid-1980s
species.keySource: BTO Breeding Bird Survey; BoCC5 (2021)

conservationStatus.trendDetail: −33–41% over 25 years (Barnes et al. 2023); 42% of UK farmland may lack key species

species.tagline: The invisible foundation — declining unseen beneath our feet
species.description: Earthworms are arguably the most ecologically important animal in this entire network. They engineer soil structure through burrowing, recycle nutrients through decomposition, improve drainage, and boost plant production by an average of 25%. They are the primary food source for badgers (80% of diet), hedgehogs, foxes, tawny owls, barn owls, skylarks, and frogs. Their 33–41% decline over 25 years threatens the entire terrestrial food web from the bottom up.
species.keyFact: Earthworms contribute an estimated 6.5% of global grain production (~140 million tonnes annually)
species.keySource: Barnes et al. (2023) PLOS ONE — first century-scale UK meta-analysis

conservationStatus.trendDetail: Hedgerow loss has slowed but 50% lost since 1945

species.tagline: The hedgerow backbone — 150+ insect species depend on a single bush
species.description: Hawthorn is the defining species of British hedgerows, supporting over 150 insect species. Its dense thorny structure provides critical shelter and nesting habitat for hedgehogs, hibernation sites, and corridors connecting fragmented habitats. May blossom provides nectar for emerging bumblebee queens and butterflies. Haws feed thrushes, jays, and foxes through autumn and winter. Britain has lost approximately half its hedgerows since 1945.
species.keyFact: Supports over 150 different insect species
species.keySource: Woodland Trust species profile; Defra Hedgerow Survey

conservationStatus.trendDetail: −63% over three generations; classified Endangered in GB (2023)

species.tagline: A living nutrient pipeline between ocean and river — now Endangered
species.description: Atlantic salmon are anadromous fish that feed at sea and spawn in freshwater, serving as a living nutrient pipeline. Their carcasses deliver marine-derived nitrogen and phosphorus to nutrient-poor upland rivers — a process traced through 2,000 years of sediment records. Their 63% decline severs this cross-ecosystem connection, creating 'cultural oligotrophication' that cascades to aquatic invertebrates, otters, kingfishers, and riparian vegetation.
species.keyFact: Salmon carcasses deliver marine-derived nutrients traced through 2,000 years of river sediment
species.keySource: Sheringham et al. (2022) The Holocene; Bernthal et al. (2022) Aquatic Conservation

conservationStatus.trendDetail: Recovered from near-extinction; now present in every English county

species.tagline: A comeback story that's saving other species along the way
species.description: Once nearly extinct in England due to organochlorine pesticides, the otter has staged a remarkable recovery and is now found in every English county. As the apex freshwater predator, its return creates positive cascade effects: otters displace invasive American mink (reducing mink occupancy from 77% to 23% within one year), indirectly benefiting water voles, kingfishers, and other species devastated by mink predation.
species.keyFact: Otter recovery reduced mink site occupancy from 77% to 23% in the Upper Thames within one year
species.conservationOrg: Wildlife Trusts / UK Wild Otter Trust
species.keySource: Bonesi & Macdonald (2004) Oikos 106:9–18; McDonald et al. (2007) Diversity & Distributions

conservationStatus.uk: WCA Schedule 5, Habitats Directive Annex II
conservationStatus.trendDetail: −50–80% decline; displaced by invasive signal crayfish carrying crayfish plague

species.tagline: Britain's only native crayfish — displaced by an invasive cousin carrying plague
species.description: The white-clawed crayfish is Britain's only native freshwater crayfish and is now Endangered globally. Invasive North American signal crayfish carry crayfish plague (Aphanomyces astaci), which is 100% lethal to native crayfish. Signal crayfish also outcompete native crayfish for food and shelter, and their aggressive burrowing destabilises riverbanks. Native crayfish are now confined to fragmented headwater refugia.
species.keyFact: Crayfish plague carried by signal crayfish is 100% lethal to the native species
species.keySource: IUCN Red List assessment; Holdich et al. (2009) Knowledge & Management of Aquatic Ecosystems

conservationStatus.trendDetail: Population fluctuates with winter severity; benefits from mink decline

species.tagline: A flash of electric blue — thriving where rivers are healthy
species.description: The kingfisher is one of Britain's most dazzling birds, nesting in earth banks along clean rivers and streams. It feeds primarily on small fish and tadpoles, and is vulnerable to both harsh winters and riverbank disturbance. Kingfishers benefit from otter recovery (which displaces mink — a predator of bank-nesting birds) and serve as indicators of freshwater ecosystem health.
species.keyFact: Kingfishers benefit from otter recovery displacing mink from riverbanks
species.keySource: BTO Breeding Bird Survey; ZSL water programme

conservationStatus.trendDetail: −94% decline; fastest mammal decline in British history

species.tagline: The fastest mammal decline in British history — 94% lost
species.description: Water voles have suffered the most rapid mammalian decline ever recorded in Britain, driven primarily by predation from invasive American mink. They are 'mini-ecosystem engineers' — eating 80% of their body weight in vegetation daily and creating diverse riverbank habitat structure through grazing and burrowing. Their loss simplifies riparian ecosystems, with knock-on effects for invertebrates, amphibians, and nesting birds.
species.keyFact: Population fell from ~8 million to fewer than 186,000 — a 94% decline
species.keySource: Rushton et al. (2000) Journal of Applied Ecology 37:475–490

conservationStatus.trendDetail: One in four UK puffins lost since 2000; globally Vulnerable

species.tagline: One in four lost since 2000 — starving as sand eels vanish
species.description: Puffins are among the most recognisable seabirds on Earth and one of Britain's most beloved wildlife spectacles. They depend almost entirely on sand eels to feed their single chick each year. As North Sea temperatures rise and sand eel populations decline, puffin chicks are starving in their burrows. The species is now globally Vulnerable — a status shared with polar bears and snow leopards.
species.keyFact: BTO models predict a potential 90% decline in puffin numbers by 2050
species.keySource: Seabirds Count (JNCC, 2023); RSPB Revive Our Seas (2021)

conservationStatus.trendDetail: UK hosts ~40% of world population; stable due to dietary flexibility

species.tagline: Britain hosts 40% of the world's grey seals
species.description: The UK hosts approximately 40% of the global grey seal population, making their conservation of international significance. Grey seals are dietary generalists, feeding on sand eels, gadid fish, salmon, and various flatfish. Their dietary flexibility has buffered them from the sand eel decline that devastated specialist feeders like puffins — illustrating how generalism provides resilience in changing ecosystems.
species.keyFact: UK hosts approximately 40% of the world's grey seal population
species.keySource: Sea Mammal Research Unit (SMRU) diet studies

conservationStatus.trendDetail: Declining due to warming seas and historic overfishing; UK banned industrial fishing 2024

species.tagline: The tiny fish holding up the entire North Sea food web
species.description: Sand eels are small, cold-water fish that form the critical prey base of the North Sea food web. They connect upward to puffins, kittiwakes, guillemots, grey seals, harbour porpoises, minke whales, cod, and salmon. Their decline — driven by warming seas shifting plankton communities and historic industrial fishing of ~1 million tonnes per year — has triggered seabird colony collapses across northern Europe. The UK banned industrial sand eel fishing in 2024.
species.keyFact: Industrial sand eel fishing in the North Sea historically removed ~1 million tonnes per year
species.keySource: RSPB Revive Our Seas (2021); Seabirds Count (JNCC, 2023)

conservationStatus.trendDetail: Only 4–12 nesting attempts in England annually vs 300+ habitat capacity

species.tagline: England could support 300+ pairs — illegal persecution limits them to a handful
species.description: The hen harrier is one of England's most persecuted birds of prey. Despite legal protection since 1954, illegal killing on grouse moors suppresses the population to a fraction of habitat capacity. The ecological paradox: grouse moor management (heather burning, predator control) creates the habitat structure harriers need to breed, while simultaneously incentivising their persecution to protect grouse shooting revenue.
species.keyFact: England has habitat for 300+ nesting pairs but only 4–12 nesting attempts occur annually
species.keySource: Thirgood & Redpath (2008) Journal of Applied Ecology 45:982–991

conservationStatus.trendDetail: −31% in recent BBS period; dependent on managed heather moorland

species.tagline: Britain's only endemic bird subspecies — entirely dependent on heather
species.description: The red grouse is Britain's only endemic bird subspecies, found nowhere else on Earth. It is almost entirely dependent on heather for food (~90% of adult diet) and nesting cover. The management of grouse moors — rotational heather burning, predator control — shapes entire upland landscapes and creates a complex socio-ecological system where conservation and commercial shooting interests both depend on the same habitat.
species.keyFact: Britain's only endemic bird subspecies — found nowhere else on Earth
species.keySource: Hudson (1986) Red Grouse, Game Conservancy Trust

conservationStatus.trendDetail: Only 25% of UK peatlands in good ecological condition

species.tagline: The purple foundation of Britain's uplands — and a pharmacy for bees
species.description: Heather dominates Britain's upland moorlands and is the habitat foundation for a distinctive ecosystem. It provides ~90% of red grouse diet, nesting cover for hen harriers, and critical late-season nectar for bumblebees. Research from Kew has shown that heather nectar contains compounds that protect bumblebees from gut parasites — it's literally medicine for pollinators. Only 25% of UK peatlands are in good ecological condition.
species.keyFact: Heather nectar contains compounds that protect bumblebees from gut parasites
species.keySource: Koch et al. Current Biology (Kew heather-bumblebee research)

conservationStatus.trendDetail: One of few thriving generalist bumblebees; masks collapse of specialists

species.tagline: A pollinator success story that masks the collapse of its specialist cousins
species.description: The buff-tailed bumblebee is one of Britain's most common and recognisable pollinators, visiting a wide range of flowering plants from early spring through autumn. As a generalist, it has adapted well to urban gardens and farmland. However, its continued success masks the broader pollinator crisis: one-third of British bee and hoverfly species have experienced distribution declines, and two bumblebee species are already extinct in the UK.
species.keyFact: One-third of British bee and hoverfly species have experienced distribution declines since 1980
species.keySource: Powney et al. (2019) Nature Communications 10:1018

conservationStatus.trendDetail: −86% since 1976; one of Britain's fastest butterfly declines

species.tagline: Once everywhere, now vanishing — an 86% crash in a 'common' butterfly
species.description: The small tortoiseshell was once one of the most familiar butterflies in British gardens. Its 86% decline since 1976 shocked conservationists because it was considered a common, resilient species. Causes include a parasitic fly (Sturmia bella) that arrived from continental Europe, loss of nettle patches where caterpillars feed, and broader insect decline. Its crash demonstrates that even 'common' species can collapse rapidly.
species.keyFact: Population has crashed 86% since 1976 despite being considered 'common'
species.keySource: UK Butterfly Monitoring Scheme; Butterfly Conservation

conservationStatus.trendDetail: −60% since 1995; losing nest sites in renovated buildings

species.tagline: Screaming over rooftops for millions of years — now losing their homes
species.description: Swifts spend almost their entire lives airborne, sleeping, feeding, and even mating on the wing. They arrive in the UK each May to breed, nesting in crevices of old buildings. Their 60% decline is driven by two converging forces: loss of nest sites through building renovation and new construction without swift bricks, and decline of aerial insects (their sole food). A swift can fly 200,000km per year — the equivalent of flying to the Moon and back.
species.keyFact: A swift can fly 200,000km per year — equivalent to flying to the Moon and back
species.keySource: BTO Breeding Bird Survey; BoCC5 (2021)

conservationStatus.trendDetail: −48% in rural areas; urban populations stable

species.tagline: Britain's most adaptable predator — connecting every ecosystem
species.description: The red fox is the supreme ecological generalist, equally at home in ancient woodland, farmland, upland moors, and city centres. With 10 connections in this network, it bridges more ecosystems than any other predator. It preys on hedgehogs, frogs, squirrels, grouse, and skylarks while consuming vast quantities of earthworms and scavenging widely. Rural populations have declined 48%, altering predator-prey dynamics across multiple habitats.
species.keyFact: Earthworms can provide up to 60% of caloric intake in some conditions
species.keySource: Harris (1981) Mammal Review; Wildlife Online

conservationStatus.trendDetail: Rural populations declining; urban garden populations more stable

species.tagline: The bridge between water and land — connecting two worlds
species.description: The common frog is one of the most ecologically connected species in the UK. As an amphibian, it physically bridges freshwater and terrestrial ecosystems — breeding in ponds but spending most of its adult life on land. It is prey for otters, foxes, badgers, tawny owls, barn owls, and mink, while itself consuming earthworms and insects. With 8 network connections, it is a critical node whose decline would ripple through multiple food chains.
species.keyFact: With 8 network connections, the common frog bridges freshwater and terrestrial food webs
species.keySource: Froglife; Arnold & Burton (1978) Field Guide to Reptiles and Amphibians

conservationStatus.trendDetail: Declining as otters recover; targeted by eradication programmes

species.tagline: The fur farm escapee that triggered Britain's fastest mammal decline
species.description: American mink escaped and were released from fur farms throughout the 20th century, establishing feral populations across nearly all of Britain. Female mink are small enough to enter water vole burrows — driving the 94% water vole decline, the fastest mammal decline in British history. They also predate kingfishers, moorhens, and amphibians. Encouragingly, otter recovery is naturally suppressing mink populations as the larger native predator reclaims its territory.
species.keyFact: Female mink are small enough to enter water vole burrows and kill mothers with pups
species.keySource: Rushton et al. (2000) J Applied Ecology; Bonesi & Macdonald (2004) Oikos
